papers.title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
papers.abstract_en: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

papers.title: AutoE2E: Don't speak - Language free end-to-end autonomy A Real-Time Driving Model for L2++ ADAS and L4 Robotaxis
papers.abstract_en: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.

papers.title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
papers.abstract_en: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

papers.title: ProxySearch: Decoupled Inference-Time Scaling for Diffusion Models via Asymmetric Noise-Rank Transfer
papers.abstract_en: Noise search at inference time improves text-to-image diffusion but requires many multi-step teacher rollouts per query. Distilled few-step models are now routinely released, yet their potential as proxies inside noise search is uncharacterized. We measure proxy-teacher rank agreement across three distillation regimes and three backbones (DiT, MMDiT, UNet) and find a sharp asymmetry. On our main pool, closed-form image statistics transfer from the proxy to the teacher (Spearman $ρ$ up to 0.80), while learned semantic scorers do not ($ρ\le$ 0.12). Paired null controls trace this rank to the first denoising step for coarse statistics and to distillation for finer ones. We use the asymmetry for noise search under a joint constraint: a semantic reward specifies content, and a numeric target specifies image statistics. In PROXYSEARCH, the proxy filters candidates by statistical match in 1 step, and the teacher returns the survivor with the highest semantic reward. No weight trades one objective against the other. On FLUX-1024, PROXYSEARCH tightens the statistical target by 21-23% at the same number of teacher trajectories, with no detected loss on the optimized reward.

papers.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
papers.abstract_en: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

papers.title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract_en: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

papers.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract_en: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

papers.title: Understanding Cross-Modal Inconsistency through Representation Subspaces in Omni Models
papers.abstract_en: Omni Models process audio, vision, and text within a unified language backbone, yet often produce different answers for semantically equivalent inputs across modalities. Existing representation-level analyses do not distinguish between information that predicts whether disagreement will occur and the representation whose perturbation affects the model's answer. In this paper, we estimate a low-dimensional Answer Subspace from answer-position representations and use it to separate answer-related components from the remaining representation. Across three Omni Models and two multimodal reasoning tasks, information predictive of cross-modal inconsistency lies mainly outside the Answer Subspace, concentrating in a reproducible two-dimensional representation that is not explained by a fixed modality offset. Matched interventions reveal distinct behavioral roles: perturbing the Answer Subspace substantially changes the model's predictions, whereas perturbing the disagreement representation, like a random subspace of the same dimensionality, leaves them almost unchanged. Our key finding is that cross-modal disagreement can be induced by misaligning modality-specific answer representations: perturbing the Answer Subspace for only one modality induces disagreement, whereas applying the same perturbation to both largely preserves agreement. Thus, the representation that predicts disagreement is distinct from the answer-level representation through which disagreement can be induced, showing that linear decodability does not imply behavioral efficacy.

papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.abstract_en: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

papers.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
papers.abstract_en: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

papers.title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?
papers.abstract_en: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.

papers.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
papers.abstract_en: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

papers.title: It Depends on the Task: Rethinking Rhetorical Segmentation of Dutch Judicial Decisions
papers.abstract_en: Classifying the material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision (rhetorical roles) in case law is a prerequisite for high-quality performance across virtually all NLP-in-law tasks, including legal information retrieval, summarisation, and LLM-based analysis. These rhetorical roles often intertwine and shift sentence by sentence, making reliable classification difficult. This paper introduces the first sentence-level annotated dataset of Dutch judicial decisions, labelled across four legally meaningful categories: material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision, alongside non-annotated (None) content, and compares several classification strategies, including a staged pipeline that separates None detection from the rhetorical roles, and a Bayesian update that leverages information about the section-header a sentence belongs to. Our results show that no single strategy dominates on both precision and recall: header priors help most when the None sentences are excluded and offer little benefit for None detection itself. These trade-offs matter in practice. For instance, extractive summarisation depends more on recall so it does not miss relevant facts, whereas outcome prediction depends more on precision regarding decision and facts sentences so that the predicted ruling is not contaminated by noise. We use these trade-offs and map the approaches tested in this study onto a set of representative legal NLP use cases.

papers.title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
papers.abstract_en: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
papers.abstract_en: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

papers.title: UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations
papers.abstract_en: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.

papers.title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract_en: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.

papers.title: FrameRouter: Frame Budget Routing for Long-Video Understanding on Video-MME-v2 and Beyond
papers.abstract_en: Long-video question answering benchmarks like Video-MME-v2 typically evaluate systems under a uniform frame budget for every question, despite stark variation in the evidence each query actually demands. We analyze this mismatch on Video-MME-v2 and find that different question subsets prefer different frozen frame-budget policies, while uniformly increasing the frame count does not reliably improve all metrics. These findings motivate fixed-mean frame-budget routing, a controlled inference setting in which each question may receive a different frame budget while the average budget matches a uniform reference. We introduce FrameRouter, a training-free test-time framework that combines an evidence-demand router, a budget-constrained allocation rule, and a frozen bank of frame-sampling policies. By controlling how much visual evidence each question receives while leaving the underlying samplers unchanged, FrameRouter is orthogonal to query-aware frame selection. Across Video-MME-v2 and several long-video understanding benchmarks, FrameRouter improves long-video question answering by using the same average visual budget more selectively across questions. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/FrameRouter.

papers.title: Storing the Gemma 4 K=V Cache Once: Exact Global-KV Memory Savings in a Paged Serving Engine with Unchanged Attention Kernels
papers.abstract_en: In the global attention layers of Gemma 4 31B, the value is the normalized key projection, and the key is the value scaled by a fixed weight, with rotary position encoding on one quarter of its dimensions. The Gemma 4 report states that this design reduces the global KV cache by up to 37.5%, but the open serving engines that we checked still store a full key and a full value: 1,024 values per KV head and token. We store one 640-value row instead, exact in real arithmetic, and an unchanged paged attention kernel reads it through two overlapping strided views as its key cache and its value cache. In a vLLM prototype with the 16-bit 31B model, the outputs are bit-identical to an emulation of the same arithmetic on the stock cache, 2 of 432 final answers differ from the stock engine (within its run-to-run noise), and the steady decode KV memory per request falls by a factor of 1.34 to 1.40 at 32K to 64K tokens. On a prefill/decode pair of two A100 GPUs with NIXL transfer and CPU offload, a decode engine with a full 15 GiB pool ran 1.38 times the stock decode tokens per step for 16K-token prompts (repeated to 0.06%) and 1.24 times for 8K-token prompts; a model of the vLLM block pool predicted both ratios to within 1% (the engine was 0.7% to 0.9% higher) and matched the change between them. The eager decode throughput rose by 1.30 and 1.11 times, and on this path the compact engine gave the same output tokens as the emulation for 8 prompts at batch 1. The run-time prototype makes an eager step 4% to 9% slower at equal batch, and the method does not yet stack with an 8-bit KV cache at the default scale.

papers.title: The Rhythm of Generated Video: Latent Chunking Leaves Periodic Traces in Compressed Bitstreams
papers.abstract_en: Most AI-generated video detectors analyze decoded pixels and overlook how videos are produced. We show that causal video autoencoders leave an architecture-specific rhythm in compressed bitstreams: their temporal stride concentrates unpredictable content at latent-chunk boundaries, so rate-distortion optimized encoders allocate bits periodically. Without decoding pixels, we observe four-frame pulses in CogVideoX and Wan2.2 and eight-frame pulses in LTX-Video, which are absent from content-matched camera footage. Passing camera footage through a generator's autoencoder alone induces the pulse, supporting its proposed origin. A training-free peak-ratio statistic separates generated from camera video (AUC 0.84-0.94) and persists across tested quantization settings and H.264/H.265 encoding. Frame-size traces also identify four commercial generators, with 89.2%, 84.1%, and 83.0% accuracy under H.264, H.265, and AV1, beating the pixel-based UnivFD baseline (72.7-73.6%). Our results directly link generative architecture to measurable coding demand.

papers.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
papers.abstract_en: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

papers.title: The Between-Round Decision in Autonomous Research: An LLM Controller That Reads the Whole Trajectory
papers.abstract_en: Executing an idea often changes how promising it looks, so the next step in autonomous research should rest on results, not on proposals. After each round of experiments, the system must decide whether to refine the best solution or start a new direction, which solution to build from, and what goal to set. We call this the between-round decision. Existing systems wrap it in machinery such as rules, scores, search trees, and schedules; where an LLM makes it, what the LLM needs to read is left open. We ask whether an LLM can make this decision from accumulated evidence, without a search structure around it, and how much of that evidence it needs to read. We present BRED (Between-Round Evidence-based Decision), an LLM-based controller that maintains the best verified solution so far (the Champion) and a log of past rounds, and makes one decision per round. On three widely used research-agent benchmark tasks, BRED improves on the task baselines by 4.80% in MAE on ETTh1 (to 0.4172) and by 3.44 and 3.43 points of accuracy on SST-2 (to 95.07%) and CIFAR-100 (to 84.63%), ahead of the published results. When the controller does not read the accumulated evidence, the same loop gains less: with no history it reaches 0.4299 on ETTh1 and 83.71% on CIFAR-100, whereas the full controller's MAE is 2.95% lower and its accuracy 0.92 points higher. On a new task, speech-based depression detection under a leakage-free protocol, it reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6164 on seeds held out from selection, 5.5 points above its baseline and 4.0 above the strongest published system. Code is available at https://github.com/learninginvision/BRED.

papers.title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
papers.abstract_en: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

papers.title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
papers.abstract_en: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

papers.title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
papers.abstract_en: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

papers.title: Can AI Understand Indonesian Children's Book Illustrations? Compliance, Safety, and the Cultural Alignment Gap
papers.abstract_en: Children's book illustrations carry developmental, pedagogical, and cultural responsibilities that are often formally codified in guidelines. As AI systems begin entering children's publishing pipelines, both as evaluators and as generators, a natural question arises: can they reliably meet the structural, safety, and cultural standards required? We investigate this across three criteria: guideline compliance, safety, and cultural alignment, using Indonesia's Book Leveling Guideline as a government-issued evaluation framework with explicit visual criteria for four reading levels. To understand how well VLMs can identify and apply these guideline criteria, we first evaluate them on real published children's book pages and compare their assessments against a human baseline. To then examine whether AI-generated illustrations meet the same standards, we apply the VLM judge to images produced by two generation models and cross-check them against a subset of human illustrator raters. We find that VLMs are reliable on explicit criteria such as compliance and safety, but fall short on cultural alignment, systematically missing content that human raters flag as culturally inappropriate. AI-generated illustrations show the same blind spot: they satisfy structural and safety criteria but fail to capture implicit cultural details that human raters consistently identify.

papers.title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
papers.abstract_en: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.

papers.title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings
papers.abstract_en: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the $(k+q)$-th power of its size, where $k$ is the dimension of the integration domain and $q$ is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
papers.abstract_en: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

papers.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
papers.abstract_en: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

papers.title: What Survival Benchmarks Don't Tell You: Impact of Model Selection and Dataset Regimes
papers.abstract_en: Despite the proliferation of survival analysis methods, current benchmarks often operate under narrow conditions: they heavily rely on the concordance index (C-index) for evaluation and model selection, and frequently either exclude deep learning (DL) methods or underrepresent challenging dataset regimes. To address these limitations, we conduct a large-scale, neutral benchmark comparing 10 classical, tree-based, and DL methods across 49 diverse datasets. Crucially, we treat the model selection criterion (optimizing for C-index, Integrated Brier Score (IBS), or Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO)) as an independent experimental variable. Using Bayesian mixed-effects modeling, we demonstrate that evaluation design heavily dictates conclusions. For complex DL and tree-based architectures, selecting hyperparameters to optimize for IBS instead of C-index yields substantial improvements in probabilistic accuracy and calibration at a negligible cost to discriminative ranking. Furthermore, method performance (C-index, IBS, MAE-PO, and X-CAL) is fundamentally governed by dataset characteristics. While DL models scale exceptionally well with larger sample sizes, they suffer notable performance drops in high-dimensional feature spaces. Additionally, we expose a structural vulnerability where heavy censoring artificially inflates absolute calibration metrics, creating overly conservative tests. Ultimately, our findings challenge the utility of global single-number performance summaries and advocate for survival analysis results that transparently report the evaluation setup. Our code is available at: https://github.com/sdening/surv-bench-study

papers.title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation
papers.abstract_en: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts $c_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p_i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F_m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.

papers.title: LLMs as Validators for Cross-Chain Bridges: Evaluating Source-Level and Transaction-Level Attack Detection on Solana
papers.abstract_en: Cross-chain bridges have suffered substantial asset losses due to vulnerabilities in their on-chain programs. On Solana, missing validation checks can enable exploits even when the underlying blockchain operates correctly. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to diagnose these flaws from source code or transaction records, rather than merely raise alarms, remains insufficiently understood. We implement a native Rust lock-and-mint bridge on a local Solana validator with four exploitable variants: two model flaws from the Cashio and Wormhole incidents, while the other two represent vulnerability classes documented in Solana security audits. Paired vulnerable and secure programs, together with successful attacks, benign sessions, and blocked attempts, allow us to distinguish correct diagnoses from unsupported alarms. We evaluate six configurations of five open-weight models across 16,800 responses, compare source inputs with and without comments, and grade 7,200 answers on vulnerable inputs using two blinded LLM graders. The results reveal substantial differences across conditions: without comments, models diagnose 24% of vulnerable source inputs while frequently flagging the secure bridge. Transaction diagnosis is high for the missing-signer scenario but averages 6% across the other three scenarios. Original comments, some of which describe the flaw, increase source diagnosis to 60%. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing correct vulnerability diagnoses from unsupported alarms in bridge security review.

papers.title: PhysResponse: Probing the Physics of Video Generation with Controlled Interventions
papers.abstract_en: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. Evaluating ten image-to-video models, we find that even the lowest parameter errors exceed those of physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude, that models rarely reproduce both outcomes of a transition pair, and that the two levels expose complementary failures that visual metrics such as PSNR miss. To supply the missing training signal, we construct 72,000 simulated videos of 20 multi-object interaction types with controlled parameters; fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors, even on held-out interaction types, and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. Continued training with a numerical encoder further lowers all three errors on held-out types. PhysResponse provides a foundation for world simulators that follow physical conditions, not just appearances.

papers.title: LIC-Audit: How Comparable Are Reported Gains in Learned Image Compression?
papers.abstract_en: Learned image compression (LIC) papers often report BD-rate improvements of only a few percent. They are measured against VTM reference software whose version keeps changing: the claims we audit name 7 versions, 5 in 2025 papers alone. But how comparable are these numbers across papers, and what evidence should future papers give for such small gains? We introduce LIC-Audit, an analysis of 353 released rate-distortion curves from 36 repositories, and a controlled re-evaluation of eight public codec releases with 28,193 encode-decode records. We identify three problems. First, different VTM reference runs change BD-rates by up to 3.56 percentage points, and on CLIC Pro published numbers order 10 of 55 method pairs differently from a common computation; comparing codecs directly over a fixed quality range removes this dependence. Second, releases use different and mostly undocumented conventions for counting bits, computing PSNR, and padding images. Under consistent measurement, the GLIC method's 1.00% lead over the HPCM method on Tecnick becomes a 1.43% deficit, changing only the padding reverses the comparison of HPCM and CMIC, and most gaps narrow when MS-SSIM replaces PSNR. Third, average curves hide how much results vary from image to image, so whether a small gain is statistically significant depends on the assumed variation. An optimistic assumption calls 12.0% of comparisons between equally good codecs significant on test sets as small as Kodak, instead of 5%; a cautious one leaves 18 of 45 differences between recent codecs undecided, yet per-image results show 12 of them to be significant. Beyond auditing past results, LIC-Audit provides a versioned evaluation protocol, a public leaderboard website with a scoring tool, source-linked benchmark data, per-image measurements, and reporting guidelines, to help future LIC papers make comparable and verifiable claims of progress.

papers.title: SOTA or Luck? The Winner's Curse in LLM Leaderboards
papers.abstract_en: Public LLM leaderboards guide model evaluation and adoption, yet the reported performance of top-ranked models can be systematically overstated. This leaderboard winner's curse arises because ranking noisy benchmark scores rewards sampling luck alongside genuine ability. The same selection effect can distort scores throughout the leaderboard, a phenomenon we call the rank-induced bias. We develop an $m$-out-of-$N$ bootstrap to correct for this bias. It assumes a fixed model pool with independent, identically distributed bounded tasks while allowing arbitrary within-task correlation among models. Under exact population tiers separated by positive gaps, we prove that the bootstrap reduces $Θ(N^{-1/2})$ ranking bias to expected residual bias $o(N^{-1/2})$. Across 14 benchmarks from 5 benchmark families, the rank-1 adjustments range from approximately 0.09 to 3.86 percentage points. In our SWE-bench Verified snapshot, the tied leaders receive an adjustment of 0.90 percentage points. Such overstatement is large enough to make the apparent winner statistically fragile. Thus, we use the same bootstrap to further quantify the intervals of plausible rank positions for each model and group models into tiers. We establish sufficient conditions for consistent recovery of population tiers. On SWE-bench Verified, this procedure places 13 of 173 models in the leading tier. We combine the score adjustment and rank intervals in the Rank Uncertainty and Leaderboard Evaluation Report (RULER). We validate its finite-sample performance using sample splitting and calibrated simulations, and advocate publishing RULER alongside raw rankings so readers can assess both reported performance and the precision of the ordering. RULER also provides guidance for benchmark design that accounts for selection effects and ranking uncertainty.

papers.title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
papers.abstract_en: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.

papers.title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
papers.abstract_en: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

papers.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
papers.abstract_en: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.

papers.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
papers.abstract_en: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

papers.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
papers.abstract_en: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

papers.title: A Generative Model for Higher-Order Network Dynamics
papers.abstract_en: Conventional network representations inferred from multivariate time series describe statistical relationships between pairs of components, even when the underlying dynamics involve group interactions that cannot be represented by pairwise interactions alone. Several multivariate information-theoretic measures have been proposed to characterise dependence beyond pairs. However, due to a lack of systems with known generating mechanisms, these measures have not been carefully validated or compared for empirical use. To address this, we here introduce a generative model of stochastic network dynamics with pairwise and higher-order interactions specified by the user. The higher-order interactions are represented by directed hyperedges, and the model provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating information-theoretic measures. Removing only the higher-order term gives a pairwise-only reference. The experiments test whether a measure detects changes induced by the higher-order term relative to this reference and recovers the participating nodes and their source-target roles. A separate experiment tests discrimination between a product coupling and a specified nonlinear pairwise control, with equal root-mean-square coupling magnitude under the pairwise-only reference. Several measures detected sufficiently strong higher-order interactions across the tested network topologies and coupling functions. In the separate discrimination experiment, the measures also separated the product coupling from the specified nonlinear pairwise control. Recovery, however, became harder as the number of candidate interactions grew. The framework therefore provides a testbed where the link between higher-order signatures and mechanisms can be tested, rather than assumed, before measures are applied to empirical data.

papers.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
papers.abstract_en: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.

papers.title: Target-Consistent Action Guidance via Semi-Unbalanced Optimal Transport for Drifting World Models
papers.abstract_en: Action-conditioned world models let robots imagine the outcomes of their actions for planning and offline policy evaluation, but these uses need many rollouts, which multi-step diffusion makes expensive. Drifting models move the iteration from inference to training and generate samples in one network pass. DriftWorld brought this paradigm to action-conditioned world models; to strengthen action following, it repels predictions from the current frame, a construction borrowed from classifier-free guidance. We show that this accentuation has a target bias: the push persists even when a prediction matches the recorded future, in kernel, balanced, and unbalanced Wasserstein drifting fields alike. We introduce Mass-Share Accentuation (MSA) to remove this bias. MSA treats the current frame as a counterfactual destination competing with the recorded future in a semi-relaxed optimal transport problem; subtracting the closed-form share of the correct future makes the guidance vanish at the target, and the remainder is shared by all predictions. We prove that the recorded future is the unique fixed point along the motion direction for collapsed predictions, and that the guidance fades with prediction error. On Push-T, Robomimic, and BridgeV2, where trained models under-react rather than overshoot, MSA improves action ranking, response slope, and moving-region error over latent-space baselines at no inference cost, though these benchmarks do not isolate bias removal as the cause.

papers.title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
papers.abstract_en: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.

papers.title: TRoPE: Topology-aware Relative Positional Encoding for 4D Generation
papers.abstract_en: Video-to-4D mesh generation has made substantial progress in recovering dynamic 3D geometry and motion from monocular videos. However, commonly used feed-forward approaches remain prone to sticking artifacts, where geodesically distant vertices move together incorrectly when they become spatially close. We attribute this failure to cross-part motion leakage: spatially nearby yet structurally distant vertices may retrieve similar motion information when motion decoding fails to distinguish spatial proximity from mesh connectivity. To address this issue, we introduce TRoPE, a topology-aware relative positional encoding that makes mesh connectivity explicit in the interaction between vertex queries and mesh-supported motion sources. TRoPE derives spectral features from the graph Laplacian and constructs pairwise topological relations from distances between multi-scale diffusion features, using these relations to modulate vertex--anchor attention through rotary phases. We further introduce a vertex-wise tail-risk objective that emphasizes persistently high-error vertices to explicitly suppress sticking artifacts. To better characterize and quantify these failures, we introduce MeshSticking-4D, a dedicated benchmark for this failure mode. Experiments on MeshSticking-4D show that TRoPE suppresses sticking artifacts while improving overall motion accuracy. Compared with the baseline, it reduces the worst-vertex error by 39.4% and lowers the separation failure rate from 49.35% to 34.90%. Additional evaluations on Motion-80 and Motion324-Subset show lower tail errors on diverse objects, while transfer to Mesh4D demonstrates applicability across backbones.

papers.title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
papers.abstract_en: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

papers.title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract_en: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

papers.title: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
papers.abstract_en: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.

papers.title: Stochastic Diversity Windows: Diagnosing Noise Influence in Robotic Diffusion Sampling
papers.abstract_en: Diffusion models are increasingly adopted in robotics and control due to their capability to express multiple feasible solutions to a given task. However, the role of stochasticity in the diffusion model-sampler across denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic that tests how changing the sampled noise affects the final output. Across five model-sampler configurations spanning three robotics benchmarks, diverse architectures, domains, and conditioning mechanisms, we reveal highly varied temporal sensitivity profiles, where noise-induced deviations can amplify, partially contract, or undergo near-total attenuation downstream. From these profiles, we define stochastic diversity windows (SDWs): compact intervals that identify where sampler stochasticity has the strongest measured influence on the final output. Guided by these windows, we apply two heuristic interventions: targeted stochastic amplification, which increases sample diversity exploration of the solution space, and an SDW-hybrid sampler, which replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions, resulting in network evaluation reductions of up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85%, with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.
